Restoration and mat removal run Q4 2027 to Q4 2028. The same application's narrative start of Q2 2026 matches the Northern Route table 1.8-1, not this Southern table.

knownCoordination.description: The PSC Final Decision in 1515-CE-103 says the approved line ends at the new 345 kV Tremval North Substation (switching station) approved in docket 5-CE-158, the Western Wisconsin Transmission Connection. It says NSPW would construct, own and operate that station. The WWTC Final Decision authorizes the Tremval North Substation Expansion site. This documents a shared interconnection facility only. It does not show joint ownership of the line or shared construction resources.

Dairyland's July 2024 application says the line would connect to a new 345 kV switching station that also connects to Xcel's Tremval-Eau Claire-Jump River (WWTC) project, and that the station location would be set in the WWTC docket. Dairyland routed to both of Xcel's preferred station sites. The final connection configuration was to be 'determined in coordination with Xcel Energy'. The application also says the station must be completed by the end of 2028 for Dairyland's connection. This documents interface design coordination only. Separately, the WWTC Final Decision lists Dairyland among the parties granted intervention in 5-CE-158; that is procedural participation, not evidence of shared resources.

No cached source documents shared crews, equipment, joint construction scheduling or joint outage plans between the Dairyland Alma-Blair and NSPW/ATC WWTC work packages. The 2024 application states only a schedule dependency (the switching station must be complete by the end of 2028). It says Dairyland will coordinate outages with MISO, and it notes that Dairyland and Xcel supplied existing-corridor widths for its impact tables. Absence here does not show a lack of coordination.

caveats: The route geometry is the PSC docket GIS centerline of the application's Proposed Southern Route (3-28-2024 alignment) plus the Segment 6 alternate end point. It is not survey accurate and may be adjusted after approval (see route.caveat). The Northern alternative was not authorized and is not traced.

The PSC Final Decision gives only a construction start (Q4 2026) and an in-service date (September 2028), not a construction end. Its start is recorded as a fact, not a construction window. The only windows with both ends come from the Dairyland page (2026-2027) and the outdated July 2024 application table (Q4 2026-Q1 2028).

The documented Xcel/NSPW interface is an interconnection at a shared switching station (Tremval North, NSPW-owned) plus interface design coordination described in the 2024 application. No source shows shared crews, equipment or other resource sharing.

The Tremval North point comes from the PSC's WWTC (5-CE-158) GIS layer for the candidate 'Tremval Expansion North' site, which the WWTC decision authorized. It marks the site, not a surveyed station footprint.
'not-found-in-sources' coordination entries mean the cached sources are silent. They do not mean the projects are uncoordinated.

knownCoordination.description: Single joint CPCN (docket 5-CE-157) with ATC; executed Common Interest, Joint Prosecution, and Confidentiality Agreement; Xcel describes construction as a collaboration between Xcel Energy and ATC. Each owner builds its own segment.

The two segments meet at a Point of Change of Ownership location agreed between NSPW and ATC; further agreements (Joint Development, Owners Coordination, Transmission-to-Transmission Interconnection, Fiber) are listed only as possible ('may include').

Joint regulatory and permitting coordination: PSC order condition 7 has the applicants work with Commission staff on an RFP for one combined independent environmental/agricultural monitor (IEM/IAM) reporting to the Commission, and the draft RFP went to both NSPW and ATC; NSPW and ATC jointly coordinated with SHPO/PSCW on the Silver Mound Historic District; the application plans outage sequencing with ATC and NSPW system operators and MISO. This is compliance and outage coordination, not documented sharing of construction crews, equipment or laydown yards.

NSPW segment starts at the Tremval Substation Expansion North (now Larkin Valley Substation), whose scope is in the Western Wisconsin docket 5-CE-158 (NSPW and ATC co-applicants); the 5-CE-158 decision authorized the North site. Shared-owner context (NSPW in both).

No cited Grid Forward source documents shared crews, equipment, laydown, outage or construction-schedule coordination with Dairyland's Alma–Blair project. Dairyland was granted intervenor status in 5-CE-157 but offered no evidence and filed no briefs, and Alma–Blair appears only as a planning-model assumption. Not evidence of no coordination.

route.description: Approved Route 2 has two segments. Segment 2A runs ~39 miles generally north from the Tremval Substation Expansion North (Larkin Valley) site near Blair to the new Elk Farm Substation in the Town of Seymour. Segment 2B runs ~41 miles: east, then north along North 90th Avenue toward STH 29, then east along the STH 29 corridor beside an existing line to Jump River Substation South in the Town of Longwood, Clark County.

route.caveat: schematic / not survey accurate. Waypoints are vertices of the Route 2 polylines (layer 39 'Transmission Route') in the PSC's docket 5-CE-158 map service, simplified with a 150 m tolerance (max deviation checked: 136 m on 2A, 122 m on 2B). This is application/proceeding-era GIS for the route the Commission authorized 'as presented'. The local alternatives in the map-service layers 'Route Adjustment 11.5' (near 190th/195th/199th Street, within about 1.5 km of the plotted line) and 'Route Adjustment 11.7' (PSCW-KF-11.7) were not merged. NSPW's Q2 2026 report says pole spotting between Elk Farm and Larkin Valley was completed in June 2026, but the 30% design package was still in progress and pole spotting for Elk Farm to Jump River was preliminary, so the final alignment may shift.

Latest owner filing (NSPW Q2 2026 progress report, filed 2026-07-27). The start is explicit. No construction end date is given, so the end bound is the in-service quarter from the same sentence. Construction could finish earlier.

knownCoordination.description: NSPW and ATC jointly applied for, and received, one CPCN in docket 5-CE-158. NSPW says it will construct, own and operate all parts except the Jump River Substation. ATC files its own quarterly reports. The NSPW line terminates at the Jump River Substation. ATC's image-only Q2 2026 cost table also lists ATC line work and items at other substations, which the NSPW statement does not reflect (see unresolved).

Dairyland's Alma-Blair 345 kV line terminates at the new Tremval North switching station approved in 5-CE-158. The 1515-CE-103 decision says NSPW constructs, owns and operates that station. Dairyland's July 2024 application said the final connection configuration would be 'determined in coordination with Xcel Energy', and that the station must be completed by the end of 2028 for Dairyland's connection. Dairyland was a granted intervenor in 5-CE-158 but offered no evidence. This is interconnection-level coordination only; no source documents shared crews, equipment or construction sequencing.

No reviewed source documents shared crews, equipment, laydown yards, outage or construction sequencing between NSPW's WWTC work and Dairyland's Alma-Blair line. Not found in sources does not mean uncoordinated.

caveats: Status 'approved' at the 2026-09-26 snapshot rests on NSPW's Q2 2026 report (filed 2026-07-27), which anticipates a Q4 2026 construction start. No later filing or news was found. The Q3 2026 report is not due until after the snapshot.
Completion claims conflict: the Xcel web page and Jan 2026 info sheet say 2027-2028, while the PSC final decision, the PSC case page and NSPW's own Q2 2026 filing say Q3 2029. Not reconciled.

Only Xcel's web page and info sheet give an explicit construction period (2026-2027). For the PSC and NSPW claims, the window's end bound is the completion or in-service quarter stated in the same sentence as the construction start, not a stated construction end.
The application-era PSC case-page schedule (construction from Q3 2025) is superseded and is not listed as a construction window; see unresolved.

The PSC final decision's cost table labels the Route 2 line costs 'ATC'. NSPW's Q2 2026 report says this is wrong and that NSPW constructs the line. Ownership here follows NSPW's filing and Xcel's page.

Larkin Valley Substation (Xcel), Larkin Valley Substation Expansion North (NSPW cost table), Tremval Substation Expansion North (PSC 5-CE-158) and 'Tremval North Substation' / 'Tremval switching station' (PSC 1515-CE-103, which also misspells it 'Tremval Nouth') are treated as the same facility, based on how the sources describe them.

The PSC's $41.9 million 'ATC Jump River Substation South' subtotal (final decision p. 52) matches ATC's substation-plus-line total ($36,107,000 + $5,745,000), so it is not the cost of the Jump River Substation alone.

relations.siteDetail: Tremval North 345 kV Substation / switching station (approved in PSC docket 5-CE-158)
relations.description: The PSC Final Decision in 1515-CE-103 says the Alma-Blair South Route ends at the 345 kV switching station approved in the WWTC docket 5-CE-158. The decision names it the Tremval North Substation, to be built, owned and operated by NSPW. The WWTC Final Decision authorizes the Tremval North Substation Expansion site. Dairyland's July 2024 application said the same new station would also connect to Xcel's Tremval-Eau Claire-Jump River (WWTC) project. In the PSC GIS layers, the Alma-Blair Segment 6 end node and the WWTC 'Tremval Expansion North' point are about 0.36 km apart.

These are separately numbered MISO LRTP Tranche 1 projects: Alma-Blair is the Wisconsin portion of Project 4, and WWTC is Project 5. The Alma-Blair decision cites WWTC as a joint NSPW/ATC CPCN application (docket 5-CE-158, cited as Wis. PSC Dec. 11, 2025; the WWTC decision itself is dated 2025-12-10). Each decision's benefit modeling was also run without the other project in service, and Dairyland intervened in 5-CE-158. They are distinct work packages with different owners, not duplicates.

relations.siteDetail: Tremval North Substation / Larkin Valley Substation (approved in 5-CE-158), near Blair

The shared site is established by this chain of decisions plus Xcel's renaming note; no single document states both lines terminate there, and Xcel's info sheet says Larkin Valley is 'near' Tremval North. Shared site is a geographic/interconnection relation, not evidence of resource sharing.

Separately numbered MISO LRTP Tranche 1 projects in separate dockets (Alma–Blair is LRTP Project 4, docket 1515-CE-103; Grid Forward is LRTP Project 6, docket 5-CE-157). Grid Forward's planning analysis assumes Alma–Blair in service as a modeling case. Portfolio membership is not a joint initiative or documented coordination. The ATC package's nearest documented point (the PCO) is ~34 mi straight-line from the existing Tremval Substation.

The Western Wisconsin project (docket 5-CE-158) is a separate LRTP Tranche 1 project; the PSC found Grid Forward beneficial individually and in conjunction with it. ATC is a co-applicant in 5-CE-158 with NSPW, so this is shared-owner context, not a cross-utility lead.

Northland terminates at the new Big Oaks Substation; Xcel Energy builds Big Oaks as part of the Alexandria-Big Oaks project (outside Northland's scope per the Biennial Report). Shared-owner context: MP and GRE own both packages.

assumptions.label: Typical easement (right-of-way) width, 115 kV line (Georgia Transmission)
assumptions.note: Georgia Transmission Corp. fact sheet (2017). The two values are the Roadside and Cross Country columns. Typical is the cross-country width, printed as '+ 100 feet'; I read that as 100 ft or more, so 100 is the conservative end. Low is the bottom of the roadside easement range (25-42.5 ft), used where a line runs beside a road right-of-way. The H-frame row also says '+ 100 feet' cross-country. The sheet gives no upper bound. As a cross-check, MISO's indicative width is 90 ft (rowWidthFt.115.miso). I found no public DESC or Georgia Power statement of a 115 kV width.

assumptions.label: Typical right-of-way width, 230 kV line (DESC / SCE&G certificate application)
assumptions.note: South Carolina Electric & Gas (now Dominion Energy South Carolina) filed this Siting Act application on July 7, 2010 (cover letter, page 2). It covers an 8.0-mile 230 kV line between two substations in northeast Columbia, Richland County (page 5), and states a typical width of 100 ft. The excerpt supports only this single value, so no low or high is given. Georgia Transmission gives 100 ft (single pole) to 125 ft (H-frame) cross-country (rowWidthFt.230.gtc). MISO's indicative width is 125 ft (rowWidthFt.230.miso).

assumptions.label: Easement width, 230 kV line, Georgia Transmission range (roadside / single pole / H-frame)
assumptions.note: Low is the bottom of the roadside single-pole easement range (25-42.5 ft). Typical is the cross-country single-pole width ('+ 100 feet'). High is the cross-country H-frame width ('+ 125 feet'). The sheet calls these values approximate.

assumptions.label: Easement width, 500 kV steel lattice line (Georgia Transmission)
assumptions.note: The sheet gives 150-180 ft cross-country and no roadside value. Typical is set to the low end of that range (150 ft) to stay conservative; I did not use a midpoint. The 100-150 ft figure in the structure-height table on the same page is a structure height, not a width. MISO's indicative width is 200 ft (rowWidthFt.500.miso). I found no public DESC 500 kV width.

assumptions.label: MISO indicative right-of-way width, 115 kV (cross-check)
assumptions.note: The feet values follow the voltage columns in order, so 115 kV = 90 ft. MISO calls these widths indicative; they are not tied to any project. Use as a cross-check only, because SC and GA are outside MISO.

assumptions.label: MISO indicative right-of-way width, 230 kV (cross-check)
assumptions.note: 230 kV = 125 ft, the same as Georgia Transmission's H-frame cross-country width. Cross-check only.

assumptions.label: MISO indicative right-of-way width, 500 kV (cross-check)
assumptions.note: 500 kV = 200 ft, wider than Georgia Transmission's 150-180 ft for steel lattice. The same page says MISO assumes steel-pole structures for all AC voltages from 69 to 765 kV. Cross-check only.

assumptions.label: South Carolina average farm real estate value, 2026
assumptions.note: pdftotext reads this table one column at a time. This run is the 2026 column, with rows in page order Southeast, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, so SC = $4,900 and GA = $4,950. Reading the South Carolina row across 2022-2026 gives 4,070 / 4,360 / 4,500 / 4,740 / 4,900, +3.4% from 2025. USDA defines farm real estate as all land and buildings on farms (page 4). The report was released July 31, 2026 (page 22). This is a statewide average, not a value for any specific corridor. Low and high were removed because the page-9 excerpt does not contain them. Bare-land alternatives from the same report are separate keys with their own verified excerpts: SC cropland $4,100 (landValuePerAcre.SC.cropland) and SC pasture $4,500 (landValuePerAcre.SC.pasture).

assumptions.label: Georgia average farm real estate value, 2026
assumptions.note: This is the same 2026 column as the SC entry (Southeast, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina), so GA = $4,950. The Georgia row reads 3,900 / 4,270 / 4,500 / 4,720 / 4,950 for 2022-2026, +4.9%. Low and high were removed because they came from other pages, not this excerpt. The alternatives are separate verified keys: GA cropland $4,670 (landValuePerAcre.GA.cropland) and GA pasture $5,100 (landValuePerAcre.GA.pasture).

assumptions.label: South Carolina average cropland value, 2026
assumptions.note: This is the 2026 column in row order Southeast, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, so SC cropland = $4,100 (+2.5%, the last value in the percent-change column).

assumptions.label: Georgia average cropland value, 2026
assumptions.note: This is the 2026 column in row order Southeast, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, so GA cropland = $4,670 (+3.3%).

assumptions.label: South Carolina average pasture value, 2026
assumptions.note: This is the 2026 column in row order Southeast, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, so SC pasture = $4,500 (+4.7%). MISO's cost guide uses the USDA pasture value as its base land cost (miso-cost-guide-mtep24, page 7).

assumptions.label: Georgia average pasture value, 2026
assumptions.note: This is the 2026 column in row order Southeast, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, so GA pasture = $5,100 (+4.1%).

assumptions.label: Right-of-way easements priced at full USDA-based land value (MISO planning convention)
assumptions.unit: fraction of land value per acre
assumptions.note: This is a planning convention, not an observed ratio of easement price to fee value. MISO says its right-of-way costs cover land easements and prices them from the USDA land value per acre (pasture; cropland = 3x pasture; urban/suburban = 5x pasture). The same page says 'All land costs are based upon the acreage of land that the new transmission line would traverse' (also verified). The guide applies no easement discount factor, so the implied share is 1.0. That share is my inference; MISO does not state it. MISO adds a separate acquisition cost per acre on top (rowAcquisitionCostPerAcre). No SC or GA source states a typical share.

assumptions.label: Example easement payment as a share of land value (Grain Belt Express, Missouri 2016)
assumptions.unit: fraction of average fee value per acre
assumptions.note: This is one developer's landowner offer, filed with the Missouri PSC as Schedule DKL-3 (June 2016), for a line with an easement 'approximately 150-200 feet wide' (page 1). It is not SC or GA and not a typical utility share. The source contradicts itself: page 2 repeats the 110% rule, but its worked example prices the easement at 100% of the stated $5,000/acre market value ('9.1 acres x $5,000 (price per acre offer) = $45,500', verified on page 2). Treat it only as evidence that easement payments can reach or exceed fee value, and use it only as a high sensitivity case.

assumptions.label: New single-circuit 115 kV line, exploratory cost per mile (MISO; Mississippi as Southeast proxy)
assumptions.unit: USD/mile (MTEP24 $: guide says data are in 2023 $, escalated 5% to 2024; incl. 30% contingency + 7.5% AFUDC)
assumptions.note: The columns are 69 / 115 / 138 / 161 / 230 / 345 / 500 / 765 kV (header verified on the same page). The second value in each row is 115 kV: typical is Mississippi, $2.2M; low is Montana, $1.8M (the table minimum, shared with North and South Dakota); high is Louisiana and Mississippi, $2.2M (the table maximum, shared with Texas). SC and GA are not MISO states; using Mississippi as the closest Southeast proxy is my choice, not the source's. The footnote reads 'Includes contingency (30%) and AFUDC (7.5%)'. MISO says these $/mile figures are built from the guide's own assumptions and cost data (page 39), and that it assumes new right-of-way for all new lines (page 7), so this per-mile cost already includes right-of-way land and acquisition. Do not add an avoided right-of-way land value on top of it. MISO also says it 'does not recommend using exploratory cost estimates for any solution idea in the regular planning cycle' (page 39).

assumptions.label: New single-circuit 230 kV line, exploratory cost per mile (MISO; Mississippi as Southeast proxy)
assumptions.unit: USD/mile (MTEP24 $: guide says data are in 2023 $, escalated 5% to 2024; incl. 30% contingency + 7.5% AFUDC)
assumptions.note: The fifth value in each row is 230 kV: typical is Mississippi, $2.6M; low is Montana, $2.0M (the table minimum, shared with North and South Dakota); high is Louisiana and Mississippi, $2.6M (the table maximum). This is a MISO-footprint proxy, not a DESC or Georgia Power figure. It includes right-of-way land and acquisition (see lineCostPerMile.115), so do not add avoided right-of-way land value on top. Compare the DESC-derived examples: lineCostPerMile.230.descNewExample (~$2.97M/mile, which also covers substation work) and lineCostPerMile.230.descRebuildExample (~$1.27M/mile).

assumptions.label: New single-circuit 500 kV line, exploratory cost per mile (MISO; Mississippi as Southeast proxy)
assumptions.unit: USD/mile (MTEP24 $: guide says data are in 2023 $, escalated 5% to 2024; incl. 30% contingency + 7.5% AFUDC)
assumptions.note: The seventh value in each row is 500 kV: typical is Mississippi, $5.0M; low is Montana, $4.1M (the table minimum, shared with North and South Dakota); high is Louisiana, $5.1M (the table maximum). This is a MISO proxy, and it includes right-of-way land and acquisition (see lineCostPerMile.115).

assumptions.label: Single-circuit 115 kV rebuild, exploratory cost per mile (MISO)
assumptions.unit: USD/mile (MTEP24 $: guide says data are in 2023 $, escalated 5% to 2024; incl. 30% contingency + 7.5% AFUDC)
assumptions.note: The columns are 69 / 115 / 138 / 161 / 230 / 345 / 500 / 765 kV, so 115 kV = $1.7M/mile. This table is not broken out by state. MISO says it 'assumes that new right-of-way is required for all projects except transmission line rebuild projects' (page 7, verified), so this figure carries no new right-of-way cost. Many DESC plan items are rebuilds; the DESC-derived Stevens Creek-Graniteville 115 kV rebuild works out to about $1.21M/mile (lineCostPerMile.115.descExample).

assumptions.label: Single-circuit 230 kV rebuild, exploratory cost per mile (MISO)
assumptions.unit: USD/mile (MTEP24 $: guide says data are in 2023 $, escalated 5% to 2024; incl. 30% contingency + 7.5% AFUDC)
assumptions.note: The fifth value is 230 kV = $1.9M/mile. MISO gives no 500 kV rebuild value (N/A). No new right-of-way is assumed for rebuilds (page 7).

assumptions.label: DESC plan example: Stevens Creek-Graniteville 115 kV rebuild, total cost / stated miles
assumptions.note: Derived: $18,200,000 / 15 miles = ~$1.21M/mile. The total is on the same page, verified separately with the excerpt 'Total $18,200,000'; it equals the sum of the yearly amounts ($100,000 + $200,000 + $9,300,000 + $8,600,000). Status is Planned, with a planned in-service date of 12/31/29 and a stated need of 'System Hardening'. This is DESC's planning estimate for one project, not a unit cost.

assumptions.label: DESC plan example: Jasper-Okatie 230 kV #2 new line, total cost / stated miles
assumptions.note: Derived: $19,280,474 / 6.5 miles = ~$2.97M/mile. The total was verified separately on page 12 with the excerpt 'Total $19,280,474'; it equals the previous-years amount ($14,303,648, printed '$14,303648') plus 2026 ($4,976,826). The scope also includes substation work ('This makes Jasper a Medium Impact substation and will require a new CIP Hut'), so this overstates the line-only cost per mile. Status is In Progress, with a planned in-service date of 12/01/2026.

assumptions.label: DESC plan example: Wateree-Killian 230 kV rebuild, total cost / stated miles
assumptions.note: Derived: $44,517,719 / 35 miles = ~$1.27M/mile. The total was verified separately with the excerpt 'Total $44,517,719' on page 45; it equals the sum of the yearly amounts. Status is Planned, with a planned in-service date of 12/31/29.

assumptions.label: Cost escalation MISO applied from 2025 to 2026 dollars (MTEP26 guide)
assumptions.note: Optional. The rate applies 'for most cost categories'; the same sentence says MISO separately benchmarked certain costs with suppliers and vendors, so it is not a uniform rate. It can move the MTEP24 per-mile values to 2026 dollars at the user's choice, but applying 4% over more than one year is my extrapolation: the source states only the 2025-to-2026 step, and MTEP24's own dollar year is ambiguous (page 2 says 2023 $, escalated 5% to 2024). The MTEP26 guide (June 10, 2026) keeps its tables in the 'Exploratory Cost Estimate Workbook for MTEP26', an xlsx the excerpt checker cannot verify, so I did not quote 2026 $/mile values.

assumptions.label: Right-of-way acquisition cost per acre, on top of land value (MISO)
assumptions.unit: USD/acre (MTEP24 $: guide says data are in 2023 $, escalated 5% to 2024)
assumptions.note: The values in each row are pasture, crop and suburban/urban right-of-way cost, then acquisition cost, then regulatory and permitting cost. Crop is 3x pasture and urban is 5x pasture ($3,045 x 3 = $9,135, x 5 = $15,225), which confirms the order. Acquisition is $14,247 in every MISO state; the Mississippi row, 'Mississippi $2,909 $8,726 $14,543 $14,247 $2,968', was also verified on page 8. The MTEP 2018 guide (miso-cost-guide-mtep18, page 16, verified) described this item, then $9,225/acre, as covering 'routing analysis, property tracts and mapping, land owner negotiations, land acquisition and condemnation fees', separate from land value. This is a MISO proxy and applies only to avoided new right-of-way acres. It is already inside the MISO new-line $/mile figures.

assumptions.label: Regulatory and permitting cost per acre of new right-of-way (MISO)
assumptions.unit: USD/acre (MTEP24 $: guide says data are in 2023 $, escalated 5% to 2024)
assumptions.note: This is the last column. It is $2,968 in most MISO states, including Mississippi, and higher in Minnesota and Wisconsin ($9,914), North Dakota ($4,957) and South Dakota ($3,977), all read from the same page. This is a MISO proxy.

assumptions.label: Mobilization/demobilization unit cost per line project, 115 kV (MISO 2018)
assumptions.unit: USD per project (2018 $, excl. overhead, contingency, AFUDC)
assumptions.note: The values follow the voltage columns in order, so 115 kV = $100,000. The section defines this as 'all the costs associated with mobilizing and demobilizing all equipment and people needed for construction of the project'. Page 15 says 'The unit costs below are all in 2018 dollars' and that they 'do not include overhead and professional services, contingency, or AFUDC' (both verified). The MTEP24 and MTEP26 guides contain no 'mobiliz' text, so this 2018 figure is the latest separately published value I found. It is a fixed cost per project, not a share of cost.

assumptions.label: Mobilization/demobilization unit cost per line project, 230 kV (MISO 2018)
assumptions.unit: USD per project (2018 $, excl. overhead, contingency, AFUDC)
assumptions.note: The fifth value is 230 kV = $200,000 (2018 $). The same caveats apply as for the 115 kV entry.

assumptions.label: Mobilization/demobilization unit cost per line project, 500 kV (MISO 2018)
assumptions.unit: USD per project (2018 $, excl. overhead, contingency, AFUDC)
assumptions.note: The seventh value is 500 kV = $300,000 (2018 $). For substations, the same guide lists $262,660 for a new site and $157,590 for an existing-site upgrade, at every voltage (page 39).

assumptions.label: Crew mobilizations avoided when two lines on shared right-of-way and structures are built together (SCE&G testimony, summarized in a joint proposed order)
assumptions.note: This is qualitative. The passage is in a Joint Proposed Order that SCE&G, the Town and the County filed for the Commission's consideration (cover letter, page 3: 'Joint Proposed Order for the Commission's consideration'). It is not an issued Commission order; the order number is blank (page 43). It summarizes testimony by SCE&G witness Mr. Young (page 51). The statement concerns two SCE&G lines, the St. George Segment and the Lake Murray Line, which 'will share the same right-of-way and the same structures'. Building both at once avoids mobilizing crews twice, so one mobilization is avoided. No dollar amount or percentage is given. It applies only when projects share work sites or structures, and no source establishes that for any DESC-Georgia Power pair. The UI must say so.

assumptions.label: Georgia ITS new transmission line miles requiring new right-of-way, 2025-2034
assumptions.note: Context for scale only, not an input to the per-pair calculation. The two column pairs are First 5 Years and Total 10 Years. Over 10 years there are 543 miles at 500 kV, 530 at 230 kV and 69 at 115 kV, 1,142 miles in all. The first-5-year total (423 miles) was removed from 'low' because it is a subset, not a lower estimate of the 10-year figure. The same table lists 982 miles to be rebuilt or reconductored on existing right-of-way over 10 years. The ITS is owned by four participants, so these miles are not Georgia Power's alone (page 6, verified: facilities 'individually owned and maintained by Georgia Power Company (GPC), Georgia Transmission Corporation (GTC), MEAG Power (MEAG) and Dalton Utilities (DU)'). The source is the public-disclosure version of the IRP appendix.

unresolved.note: plan.md hypothesis (Grid Forward vs BECI at Columbia) - what the sources support: (a) both name the 'Columbia Substation' (PSC 5-CE-157 final decision PDF pp.1, 15; PSC case page; MISO RFP slides 26-27; MGS fact sheet map); (b) MISO assigns the Columbia modification (50950) to ATC - but only in the March 2025 RFP scope slide 27, not in the January 2026 selection report; (c) MISO 'anticipates' coordination with interconnecting TOs (selection report PDF p.9 / printed 2, listed as an aspect developers should address; PDF p.36 / printed 29 on real-time operations). NOT supported by any source: an existing arrangement between the BECI developer and the Grid Forward applicants, a schedule for ATC's Columbia work, or any route. Grid Forward sources never mention BECI, 765 kV, Tranche 2.1, Transource or Sugar Creek. Keep as a needs-review lead, not a headline demo item.

The shared site is name-based: BECI sources and Grid Forward sources each say 'Columbia Substation'; neither discusses the other project. Grid Forward and the MGS map place it in Columbia County, and OSM has a single ATC 345 kV 'Columbia Station' there, so identity is very likely but not stated by a source.

Timing at Columbia: Grid Forward's PSC decision expects construction Q4 2026 - by December 2030 (PDF p.54) and to proceed from the Columbia substation north (PDF p.30); BECI's MGS schedule shows tree clearing/construction/restoration late 2029 - late 2033 (approximate, pre-CPCN). Reported windows overlap roughly late 2029-2030 ('confirmed' only if 'completion by December 2030' is encoded as ending in Dec 2030; 'possible' if 'by' is treated as an upper bound only). Whether any BECI or ATC work at the Columbia site itself happens in that overlap is unknown.

Project id 'atc-nspw-grid-forward' is a placeholder shared with the Dairyland cluster; Grid Forward's applicants are ATC, NSPW, SMMPA Wisconsin and WPPI Energy (final decision p.1), so its owner set may need more than atc/xcel-nspw. New utility ids used here: bhe-transmission, comed, gridliance-heartland.

No construction window, cost, docket or in-service date found for ATC's Columbia (50950) or Sugar Creek (51027) work, or for DPC's facilities 50948/50953. BECI's June 1, 2034 deadline applies to the three BECI lines only.

MariBell: Dairyland (May 8, 2025 release) and the MariBell site say Dairyland and GridLiance Heartland will jointly develop and co-own a 765/161 kV double-circuit line from Marion, MN to Bell Center, WI (Wisconsin segment ~32 miles in Vernon and Crawford counties along an existing corridor), the 'middle segment of the North Rochester-Columbia 765 kV line'. This very likely includes MISO facility 50948, but no source says so; GridLiance was not added as an owner and MariBell's schedule (project-details page: construction 2031-2034, in service 2034; Wisconsin CPCN filing anticipated Q4 2026) was not attached to the DPC record. Reconcile with any MariBell cluster (maribell-* sources were cached by another researcher) to avoid a duplicate work package.
No PSCW docket exists yet for BECI (MGS plans to file the CPCN in early 2027; decision anticipated summer 2028); status 'proposed'. Re-check PSC ERF after filing for route alternatives and schedule.

Date encoding is interpretive: 'Late YYYY' encoded as July-December and 'Summer' as June-September, both with precision 'quarter' as the closest enum value. MISO's 'placed into service by June 1, 2034' is a deadline encoded as a single day; it is not a forecast in-service date.

In-service claims differ: MISO/Transource require in service by 2034-06-01; AEP (Jan 2026) said the schedule is being developed to meet a 2034 in-service date; MGS (Sept 2026) shows 'Project In Service 2033'.

Route: no final route; MGS study segments (multiple alternatives) are mapped on the fact sheet and announcement packet, MISO figures are schematic, and MISO treats developers' detailed routing as confidential. County map books at static.power-viz.com/mgs-beci-mapbooks/ were not fetched. Route left unavailable.

mgs-projects.com/BECI is a JavaScript single-page app; the cached copy (mgs-beci-page) is an empty shell and is not cited. The MariBell facts formerly attributed to its FAQ are now sourced from cached Dairyland/MariBell pages instead.

IL/WI State Line point: MISO says Rock County; the MGS map shows several candidate connection points along the state line ('only one to be selected'). ComEd's IL/WI State Line - Collins 765 kV line (51029) and Collins substation work (51030) in PJM/Illinois were not modeled as projects.
Sugar Creek Substation (51027) appears in both the BECI and WISE (Viridon) RFP scopes; a WISE-to-ATC/BECI shared-site relation at Sugar Creek was not modeled here.

Counties for Sugar Creek Substation (Walworth per OSM and MGS map reading) and DPC facilities (Vernon/Crawford per geocoder and MariBell page) are not stated in the MISO source for those facilities and were omitted.

Selected Developer Agreement: the selection report says MISO and Transource will execute it within 60 days of the Jan 6, 2026 report; execution not confirmed in cached sources. The report calls the winner 'Transource, Inc.' in the summary but lists 'Transource LLC' among proposers.
The open-house boards (mgs-beci-oh-boards) are undated; their schedule board duplicates the fact sheet schedule, so they add no independent date claim.

The best non-Dairyland candidate, Xcel's Gopher to Badger Link North Rochester-Marion segment (schedule buckets 2030-2034 / 2031-2034), is about 34-37 mi straight-line from Alma (computed from OSM/Nominatim points). No non-Dairyland project within 25 mi of Alma/Blair/La Crosse/Eau Claire with a published post-2027 construction window was found.

Candidates reviewed and rejected for that row. Verified in cached mn-biennial-2025-pdf p.214 (printed 210): Xcel Rebuild Wabasha Substation (2025-SE-N11) gives only 'planned to be in service by December of 2028' (no construction window); Xcel 0774 Goodview-Str 444 rebuild (2025-SE-N10) 'expected to be completed by December of 2025'. NOT verifiable (ATC pages viewed by the researcher but not cached): Grant County Distribution Interconnection and Pittsville Area DIC schedules - treat those statements as unverified.

Gopher to Badger Link status as of 2026-09-26: the Certificate of Need (CN 25-121) was submitted; no MPUC decision was found in cached sources. The Minnesota Route Permit application was planned for 'this fall' (factsheet, map dated May 2026) and MariBell's Wisconsin CPCN for Q4 2026; neither filing is confirmed in cached sources.

POSSIBLE CROSS-CLUSTER DUPLICATE: the beci-columbia cluster's 'dpc-genoa-bell-center-765-beci-related' (MISO BECI scope 2025 p.27, facility 50948: DPC replaces existing single-circuit 161 kV structures from the MN/WI state line at the existing Genoa river crossing to near Bell Center with 161/765 kV double-circuit structures; facility 50953 Bell Center Substation) looks like MariBell's ~32-mile Wisconsin segment (Vernon and Crawford counties, existing corridor, ends at Bell Center). Hypothesis part 1 (Tremval convergence): SUPPORTED only for the NSPW-owned Grid Forward segment, not the ATC portion. Grid Forward segment 1N exits the Tremval Substation Expansion North (authorized); WWTC decision 5-CE-158 authorized the Tremval North site; Dairyland's 1515-CE-103 decision says Alma–Blair connects to the new Tremval North Substation/switching station approved in 5-CE-158; Xcel names it Larkin Valley, ~0.5 mi north of the existing Tremval Substation near Blair. The link is a chain across documents, and Xcel's info sheet says Larkin Valley is 'near' (not 'formerly') Tremval North. The ATC package's nearest documented point (PCO) is ~54 km (~34 mi) straight-line from the existing Tremval Substation, beyond the default 25-mile review radius.

Hypothesis part 2 (both publish 2026–27 construction windows): NOT CONFIRMED as stated. Dairyland's page shows construction 2026–2027 and its PSC decision says construction begins Q4 2026 with in-service September 2028. Grid Forward publishes a project-wide Q4 2026 start with completion by December 2030, not a 2026–27 window; for the Tremval-end NSPW segment, Xcel shows pre-construction ground activities 2026–2027 and general construction 2027–2030, and NSPW's Q2 2026 report moved its construction start to Q4 2027. General-construction overlap with Alma–Blair is therefore at most possible in 2027 (at the latest NSPW claim, only Q4 2027), plus pre-construction overlap in 2026–27.

Hypothesis part 3 (shared-resource plans): CONFIRMED that the cited sources do not establish Dairyland–ATC (or Dairyland–NSPW) shared crews, equipment, laydown yards or schedules. The only related statement is ATC's utility-level, planning-level 'cooperatively working on plans' among ATC, Xcel and Dairyland, which does not name Alma–Blair; it is recorded against the utility id 'dairyland' (reported-coordination, scope unknown) so it does not by itself mark the Alma–Blair pair as known coordination. The Tremval-end work belongs to NSPW (Xcel), not ATC. Status is not-found-in-sources, not 'uncoordinated'.

plan.md hypothesis check: 'Planned construction in 2026-27' is supported only by Xcel's web page ('Construction : 2026 -2027') and its Jan 2026 info sheet. The PSC final decision (start Q3 2026, completion by Q3 2029) and NSPW's Q2 2026 filing (start Q4 2026, in-service Q3 2029) imply construction running into 2029. 'Near the Dairyland project around Blair' is supported: the Alma-Blair line terminates at WWTC's Tremval North / Larkin Valley station.

Minnesota / Mississippi River end: no WWTC source describes one. WWTC runs entirely inside Wisconsin (Trempealeau, Eau Claire, Chippewa and Clark counties), from Larkin Valley/Tremval North near Blair to Jump River South. Xcel only mentions other projects 'proposed in Minnesota and to the west'. Any Mississippi crossing toward Alma belongs to other projects (e.g., Dairyland Alma-Blair).

Eau Claire Substation expansion: the docket caption still lists 'Expanding the Tremval and Eau Claire Substations', but the Eau Claire expansion was part of Route 1. The authorized Route 2 uses the new Elk Farm Substation instead, and NSPW's Q2 2026 cost table lists only Larkin Valley and Elk Farm substations. No source confirms any remaining Eau Claire Substation work under 5-CE-158.

Completion conflict (not reconciled): the Xcel web page ('Project complete: 2027 - 2028') and the Jan 2026 info sheet ('Project complete and line placed in service', 2027-2028) disagree with the PSC final decision and case page ('completion by the third quarter of 2029') and with NSPW's own Q2 2026 filing ('in-service date of third quarter 2029').

Construction start moved across claims: Q3 2025 (application era, PSC case page), then Q3 2026 (final decision), then Q4 2026 (NSPW Q2 2026 report). ATC's Jump River Substation is set for Q3 2027. The Xcel web page and info sheet show construction in 2026-2027, which conflicts with a Q3 2029 in-service date.

Removed as superseded: the PSC case page's application-era schedule ('If approved, the applicant anticipates construction for this project to begin in the third quarter of 2025 and be in-service in the third quarter of 2029') is not listed as a construction window. The same page gives the later final-decision schedule, and NSPW's Q2 2026 report shows construction had not started by mid-2026. The output schema has no supersededBy field. Its in-service claim (Q3 2029) is kept in completionClaims.

Removed from the ATC package: the final decision's project-wide schedule (construction from Q3 2026, completion by Q3 2029) is not specific to the Jump River Substation. ATC's own Q2 2026 report gives a package-specific start of Q3 2027.

Window end bounds: no source gives an explicit construction end date for NSPW's or ATC's work. The PSC and NSPW windows end at the stated completion or in-service quarter. ATC's window ends at the overall Project in-service quarter and is marked non-continuous. 'Completion by the third quarter of 2029' is encoded as Q3 2029, though 'by' permits an earlier finish.

Whether construction had actually started by 2026-09-26 is not confirmed. The latest filings are the Q2 2026 progress reports (filed July 27 and July 31, 2026), and a web search found no later construction-start notice. Q3 2026 reports are due after the quarter ends.

PSC final decision cost table (p. 52): the Route 2 transmission line and 'Other T-Line Removal/Installation' costs are labeled 'ATC'. NSPW's Q2 2026 report says this is wrong and that NSPW constructs the line. No corrected PSC table was found. The NSPW table ($438.8M) and ATC's table ($44.511M) together make up the $483.3M total.

ATC scope vs NSPW's statement: NSPW says it will 'construct, own and operate all parts of the project except the Jump River Substation'. ATC's image-only cost table (Q2 2026 report p.3, read visually, not script-verifiable) lists ATC 'Transmission Lines - South (Route 2)' ($5,745,000) and items at Gardner Park and Stone Lake substations. What that line and remote-substation work is, and where, was not determined; those sites are not mapped.

Final order date: the Xcel web page says December 11, 2025 and the Jan 2026 info sheet says December 10, 2025. The decision is signed December 10, 2025 and was PSC-received/served December 11, 2025. Xcel says verbal approval came October 30, 2025.

Docket numbering: Dairyland's July 2024 application calls WWTC 'PSCW Docket No. 4220-CE-188', while the PSC decision, the case page and the progress reports use joint docket 5-CE-158. No cached source states the renumbering; the mapping rests on the identical project name.
The PSC case page link text reads 'Docket Reports: 5-CE-185', but the link points to the ERF search for docket 5-CE-158 (SEQ=158). Treated as a typo.
ATC's Q2 2026 report says its period is 'April 1, through June 30, 2025'. Treated as a typo for 2026.

Internal text conflict in the final decision: p.15 says that after leaving W3305, Route 2 travels 'north in a single-circuit configuration for 27 miles'. p.33 says Segment 2B 'would generally parallel the existing transmission line' for about 27 miles. The PSC GIS polyline runs almost due east (about lat 44.92) from the STH 29 crossing to Jump River South, and Xcel says it generally follows State Highway 29. The GIS geometry is used.

Route geometry comes from the PSC docket map service (layer 39 'Transmission Route', application/proceeding-era GIS). The Commission approved Route 2 'as presented', but the adjustment layers 'Route Adjustment 11.5' (190th/195th/199th Street alternatives near the STH 29 crossing) and 'Route Adjustment 11.7' (PSCW-KF-11.7), the 'Structure N1-120 Option' layer, and final engineering could shift the alignment. No post-decision as-designed GIS was found. The layer list came from a live query and is not cached.
The crossing points at 250th Street (Town of Sigel) and 370th Street (Edson/Worden border) were not geocoded separately; the GIS polyline, which passes through those towns, is used instead.

Schedule dependency (not reconciled): Dairyland's July 2024 application says the new switching station must be completed by the end of 2028 for Dairyland's connection, and the 1515-CE-103 decision gives Alma-Blair a September 2028 in-service date. WWTC sources give only whole-project completion/in-service dates (Q3 2029, or 2027-2028 per Xcel) and no separate completion date for the Larkin Valley / Tremval North station.

No reviewed source documents resource sharing (crews, equipment, laydown yards, outage or construction sequencing) between NSPW and Dairyland, or between WWTC and Grid Forward. Resource-sharing status is 'not found in sources', which is not the same as 'uncoordinated'.

Owner overlap with Grid Forward: NSPW and ATC are applicants for both WWTC and Grid Forward (5-CE-157, with SMMPA and WPPI). Under plan.md section 8, a WWTC vs Grid Forward pair is shared-owner context, not a cross-utility review lead. Grid Forward also describes 'expanding the Tremval Substation', and how Tremval North / Larkin Valley work is split between 5-CE-157 and 5-CE-158 was not determined.

Cross-cluster coordinate mismatch: the Dairyland cluster places the same Tremval North switching station at the Blair locality centroid (44.2946, -91.2338, precision locality). The PSC GIS point 'Tremval Expansion North' (44.30158, -91.25420) is about 1.8 km away and should be preferred when the clusters are merged.
